title: API Rescue Blueprint — Quick Hits & Escalation Map
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, operator-focused rescue blueprint for common API degradations we see in production: timeouts, 429s (rate-limited responses), degraded streaming (partial or stalled streams), and sudden elevation in error rates. The goal is fast, repeatable mitigations + clear escalation if quick fixes fail. Treat as a pocket runbook — short commands, dashboards, and decision points.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to hosted API endpoints and Dedicated clusters surfaced in the Redwood Console.
- Assumes oncall has access to Redwood Console, PagerDuty, Grafana dashboards, and the deployment repo.
- This is not the full postmortem; after-stabilization follow the Incident Postmortem checklist.

Immediate first 6 minutes (golden minutes):
1) Identify impact surface
   - Confirm scope: number of customers affected, endpoints (text/generate, chat, embeddings, streaming).
   - Quick queries:
     - Grafana: API 5xx rate (1m/5m), 4xx breakdown, latency p50/p95/p99, streaming chunk errors.
     - Console: recent rollouts (last 30m), model variant swaps, autoscaler events.
2) Open incident channel (Slack #ops-incident-YYYYMMDD) and notify PagerDuty if not auto-triggered.
3) Short status message to channel: one-liner with what we know + action owner. Example: "Investigating elevated 5xx on /v1/generate; reverting recent canary; Diego on rollback."
4) Quick mitigation: divert traffic or lower client QoS to buy time (see mitigations below).

Quick diagnostics (one-liners to run):
- Check recent deploys: git log /deployments in console UI for last 30m.
- Check machine/instance health: kubectl get pods -n runtime -o wide | grep CrashLoopBackOff (or console node health).
- Check quota/backpressure: redis/kafka/backends showing full queues? (console metrics: request queue length).
- Streaming-specific: look for increased `stream-chunk-timeouts` and `stream-resume-failures`.

Failure-mode specific playbooks (fast path):
A) Timeouts (client RTTs or server token-generation timeouts)
- Signals: p95/p99 token gen latency spikes, grow in request queue length, increased worker GC or OOMs.
- Quick hits:
  1. Reduce per-request work: set global temp policy `max_tokens` reduction (e.g., -30%) via rate-limited config flag.
  2. Toggle model-variant to a lower-latency variant (console traffic-split to fallback model).
  3. Drain and recycle overloaded serving nodes (graceful pod restart) for nodes with high CPU steal or memory pressure.
  4. Apply autoscaler manual scale-up (add N GPUs) if capacity exhausted and safe to do so.
- Diagnostics commands/examples:
  - kubectl top pods -n runtime | sort -nr -k3
  - curl -s https://console.internal/redwood/deployments | jq '.recent[] | select(.age<1800)'
- Communication: "Mitigating by shifting traffic to fallback model and reducing max_tokens; expecting stabilization in 5–10m."

B) 429s (rate-limit/over-capacity)
- Signals: spike in 429s, per-account rate-limit counters high, quota-buckets saturated.
- Quick hits:
  1. Apply temporary soft-throttle to noisy tenants (console: tenant throttle API) — throttle by % rather than hard block.
  2. Increase global burst tokens if policy allows (short window).
  3. Activate degraded response mode: return short-circuit graceful responses with notice header (X-Redwood-Warning) for non-SLA tenants.
  4. If dedicated capacity customers only are affected, enable emergency spill to hosted pool (policy permitting).
- Diagnostics: check per-tenant request histogram and request token counters.
- Customer comms snippet: "We've detected elevated rate limits for some requests; we are applying temporary throttling to noisy clients while we restore capacity. Customers on Dedicated will be notified separately."

C) Degraded streaming (partial tokens, stalled streams, resumable failures)
- Signals: many client disconnects mid-stream, `stream-chunk-timeout` in logs, high connection resets.
- Quick hits:
  1. Shift streaming requests to chunked polling fallback (short-term): update gateway to convert streaming -> chunk-poll route for affected endpoint.
  2. Reduce stream chunk size or enable forced-flush frequency on runtime to avoid long tails.
  3. Revert any recent proxy/edge changes (NGINX, envoy listener config) that touched upstream keepalive settings.
- Diagnostics: tcpdump/conntrack checks on edge nodes, logs for `http2` resets, per-connection latency graphs.
- Note for client teams: streaming fallback will increase perceived latency for some flows but prevents full stalls.

D) Elevated error rates (5xx spikes, unknown exceptions)
- Signals: sudden rise in 5xx (500/502/503), specific exception traces in logs.
- Quick hits:
  1. Identify last change: config, model, code. Consider rollback of last deployment.
  2. If error is localized to a subset of instances, cordon & isolate them from LB.
  3. Enable fail-open paths: for non-critical features, disable model tool-calls or external integrations causing errors.
  4. If persistent unknowns, enable wide diagnostic logging with sample rate 1% (avoid full debug in prod for >10m).
- Diagnostics: grep logs for top exception stack traces, sample request IDs to replay in staging.

Escalation map (who to call after quick hits fail for >15 minutes):
- Level 1 (oncall SRE) — owner (initial responder): PagerDuty.
- Level 2 (SRE lead): Diego Morales (pager / slack DM).
- Level 3 (Runtime eng): Priya Nair — for model/runtime kernel regressions.
- Level 4 (Infra/Cloud): Samir Gupta — for capacity, autoscaler, or provider incidents.
- Exec / Customer escalation: Production Support lead (channel #prod-support-escalations).

Decision triggers for escalation:
- No stabilization after 15m of mitigations or traffic >50% degraded.
- Root cause points to code change or model rollout.
- Large-scale customer impact (10+ major customers or >5% revenue traffic).

Temporary communications templates (copy-paste friendly):
- Initial incident post to channel: "INVESTIGATING: Elevated 5xx on /v1/generate since 10:42 UTC. Scope: unknown, oncall performing model fallback + throttle. Will update in 10m."
- Customer-facing short update: "We are currently investigating degraded API responses impacting some requests. Mitigations are in progress; we expect partial restoration within ~15 minutes. We will share more details shortly."
- Customer-facing follow-up (after mitigation): "Service restored for most customers. We are continuing to monitor and will follow with a detailed incident note. If you continue to see errors, please share request IDs."

Safe rollbacks and cautions:
- Prefer traffic-split rollback (shift 100% to previous stable revision) rather than immediate deploy revert when possible.
- Avoid mass restarts during peak unless nodes are OOM/CrashLoopBackOff — restarts can amplify transient load.
- Do not increase global concurrency limits without checking downstream caches & DBs for saturation risks.

Post-stabilization checklist (first 24 hours):
- Capture timeline: events, mitigation actions, who did what (update incident doc).
- Preserve logs and set aside sample request IDs for repro.
- Create follow-up ticket for root-cause analysis and timeline to completion.
- Notify customer-success for any customers impacted with RCA and credit details if applicable.
- Schedule postmortem within 72 hours.

Notes to self / operator heuristics (things that saved time in prior incidents):
- If both latency and 429s spike together, look for a noisy tenant or a synthetic load test accidentally hitting production.
- Streaming regressions often trace back to upstream edge/library updates — check proxy changelogs first.
- Use the small toggle flags we keep in console ("reduce-max-tokens", "fallback-model") as first mitigations; they are low-risk and rollback-safe.

Known friction points to improve (action items):
- Make tenant throttle API accessible to SRE through a simplified console button (done-in-progress with UX).
- Add a single-click rollback for model-variant swaps in the Console.
- Improve visibility for streaming connection resets in Grafana (add dedicated panel).

References & quick links (save to incident doc):
- Grafana: API overview dashboard (link in console)
- Internal confluence: Incident response checklist (CON-1423)
- Runtime repo PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/992

End notes:
This is intentionally terse and operator-focused; expand with full postmortem artifacts when stable. Keep it updated with any new knobs or emergency policies we add to the Console.
